text: 原文里的「心不快」「意驕矜」「立自責」这类心理描写出自史家的叙述，本文照其叙述转述。
Phrases in the original such as "troubled in his heart," "showed a self-satisfied look" and "at once blamed himself" are the historian's narration; this piece relays them as he tells it.
本文只依据《史记·魏公子列传》；对话出自史家记述，未必逐字；「心不快」「意驕矜」「立自責」等心理描写出自史家叙述。

This piece draws only on the "Biography of the Prince of Wei" in the Records of the Grand Historian; the speeches come from the historian's account and need not be verbatim, and phrases such as "troubled in his heart," "showed a self-satisfied look" and "at once blamed himself" are the historian's narration.

魏国有位隐士侯嬴，年七十，家贫，在大梁夷门守门。无忌想厚赠他，他不肯收，说自己修身絜行几十年，终不能因为守门穷困而受财。无忌于是置酒大会宾客，空出车上左边的尊位，亲自去迎侯嬴。侯嬴穿着破旧衣冠，径直登上上座，也不谦让，为的是看无忌的反应；无忌执辔，愈恭。侯嬴又下车去见他的朋友、在市上当屠户的朱亥，故意站着和朱亥说了很久，暗中观察无忌。这时魏国的将相、宗室和宾客已坐满一堂，等无忌回去开席；跟随的骑从都在暗中骂侯嬴。无忌的脸色反而越发温和，始终不变。到家后无忌请他坐上座，向在座宾客一一介绍，宾客皆惊。侯嬴后来自己说破：他这样做是想成全公子礼贤下士的名声；市人因此把他看作小人，称无忌是能下士的长者。宴罢，侯嬴成为上客。

Wei had a recluse named Hou Ying, seventy years old and poor, a gatekeeper at the Yimen. Wuji sought him out and tried to present him with a handsome gift. Hou Ying would not take it: he had kept himself and his conduct clean for decades, he said, and would not accept the prince's money simply because gatekeeping left him poor. So Wuji laid on a feast for all his retainers, went out with his carriage and escort, left the seat of honor on the left of the chariot empty, and fetched Hou Ying himself. Hou Ying, in his shabby robe and cap, climbed straight up into that seat without a word of demur — a test of Wuji, this was — and Wuji took the reins and grew only more respectful. Hou Ying then got down to see his friend Zhu Hai, a butcher in the market, and deliberately stood talking with him for a long time, watching Wuji out of the corner of his eye. Meanwhile Wei's generals, ministers, royal kinsmen and guests filled the prince's hall, waiting for him to begin the feast, and Wuji's own riders cursed Hou Ying under their breath. Wuji's face only grew milder; his manner never changed. At the house Wuji showed Hou Ying to the seat of honor and presented him to the assembled guests one by one, and the guests were astonished. Hou Ying later spelled out his reasoning: he had acted this way to make the prince's name as a man who humbles himself before scholars. As a result, the townsfolk took Hou Ying for a lout and Wuji for a true elder who can humble himself before scholars. When the feast broke up, Hou Ying became one of Wuji's most honored guests.
